name: Nude / white waterline eyeliner

lead: Nude or white waterline eyeliner is a makeup technique where a light, skin-toned or white pencil is applied to the inner rim of the lower lid. The payoff is eyes that look brighter, larger and more awake.

The light colour counters the darker, redder rim of the lower lid, so shadow and redness at the lid margin recede and the eye appears more open. It belongs to the long tradition of eyeliner, which dates to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia. No study has tested its effect on perceived attractiveness or eye size.

paras: Users tightline or drag the pencil along the inner lower rim after drying the area, usually as a finishing step in a daily makeup routine, sometimes paired with mascara or a darker upper liner.

Anything applied to the waterline touches the eye surface; waterproof, eye-safe products are generally preferred per general makeup references. Shared or old pencils can carry bacteria. No studies of waterline-specific harms were found.

angle.text: A nude or white pencil on the lower waterline reduces the dark, red rim contrast and makes the eyes look brighter, larger and more awake as soon as it is applied. It is a popular makeup technique rather than a studied one.

lead: Nude or white waterline eyeliner is a makeup technique in which a skin-toned, beige or white pencil is applied to the lower waterline, the thin inner rim of the lower eyelid. People use it to make their eyes look brighter, more awake and larger, and to soften the look of redness or shadow along the lid margin.[1][2]

It belongs to the long history of eyeliner, which Wikipedia traces to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, where dark kohl lines were worn by men and women.[3] Makeup artists quoted in fashion and beauty media describe the light shade as making the whites of the eyes look larger against the lashes, giving a more open, rested look than dark liner on the same spot.[1][2] Nude shades are presented as a softer, less obvious option than opaque white, which reads as a more dramatic brightening.[2]

The advice comes from makeup artists, brands and users. No published study has tested nude or white waterline liner for its effect on perceived eye size or attractiveness, but related experiments have examined how eye makeup, lower-eye contrast and the visible white of the eye change how faces are judged.[4] Separate ophthalmology research has examined how eyeliner worn at the lid margin relates to tear film and meibomian gland measures.[4]

paras: The technique places a pale pencil along the lower waterline, in contrast to the dark liner traditionally used for definition. Wikipedia describes the related practice of tight lining, in which liner sits against the lash roots or waterline and makes lashes seem to begin farther back on the lid; it notes that waterproof products are generally preferred because of the eye's sensitive surface.[3]

L'Oreal Paris's beauty magazine lists the lower waterline as the main placement for nude liner, with other uses including a dab at the inner corners for a wider-eyed look, a shade lighter than skin on the center of the lid to add dimension, and a nude wing under darker shadow in place of a classic flick. It also advises avoiding heavy liner on the lower lash line to keep the eyes looking open.[2]

Waterline liners come as wax-based or mechanical pencils, gels and other formats; Wikipedia lists wax-based pencils as the cheapest and most common form of eyeliner and notes that gel liners are softer and applied with a brush.[3] The L'Oreal article lists a nude mechanical gel liner and a nude waterproof pencil among the products it mentions.[2]

Wikipedia dates eyeliner to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, saying it may have protected skin from desert sun and been worn against the evil eye, and it describes kohl made from galena and other minerals; the tomb of Nakht in Thebes (15th century BC) shows men and women wearing mesdemet kohl.[3]

In the 1960s liquid liner produced bold black and white lines in the look associated with designer Mary Quant, and later decades saw heavy liner adopted by goth, punk and emo subcultures and the early-2000s term guyliner for men wearing liner.[3] Nude and light liners on the waterline are a contrast to these dark traditions. L'Oreal's article describes nude liner under darker shadow as a retro, 1960s-inspired variation on the winged liner.[2] W Magazine's 2025 coverage of tightlining notes the technique is not new but was having a moment in 2025 with waterproof formulas and precise brushes.[1]

Brand and magazine sources describe the effects as making eyes look bigger and more open, neutralizing redness at the waterline, and giving tired eyes a more awake look.[2] Makeup artist Kasey Spickard, quoted in W Magazine, describes the contrast between the lash base and the whites of the eyes as making them look brighter and slightly larger.[1]

Artists quoted in the same coverage describe related tightlining as making lashes look fuller and, depending on placement, subtly elongating or lifting eye shapes.[1] For smaller eyes, one suggestion is to line only the outer two-thirds of the upper waterline and optionally use a nude pencil on the lower waterline; for hooded eyes the advice is to tightline instead of lining the lid and skip the lower lash line or add only a very light smudge to its outer third.[1]

sections.h: Research on eye contrast and makeup
paras: No study has tested pale waterline liner itself. Related experiments examine what the eye region contributes to how a face is judged. In a 2026 PLoS One experiment, 162 participants rated 50 neutral faces edited to show small or large scleral (white-of-the-eye) exposure; larger exposure was rated more favorably for trustworthiness, attractiveness, sociability and perceived social rank.[4] The wiki's makeup-artist sources make the same kind of claim about brighter-looking eye whites, but the experiment manipulated digital eye exposure, not makeup.

A 2018 Frontiers in Psychology study applied makeup to controlled regions of standardised grayscale female faces and compared attractiveness ratings. Adding upper-eye makeup raised attractiveness, while added contrast on the lower eyelids and lips did not, and lower-eye makeup significantly lowered ratings.[4] That study examined added contrast, which is the opposite direction from a pale liner that reduces contrast at the lower rim. A 2022 PLoS One study found subtle professionally applied makeup raised attractiveness ratings of 20 men's faces rated by 200 people, without separating out eye-region products.[4]

The tip circulates mainly in mainstream makeup coverage and tutorials, and is part of the broader set of techniques used to enhance eye area appearance, including eyebrow shaping and lash enhancement. L'Oreal's version pairs the nude liner with curled lashes, lengthening mascara and a shimmer highlight at the inner corners.[2]

Products on the waterline sit against the eye surface. Beauty sources emphasize practical points such as waterproof or waterline-specific formulas to limit smudging and wiping the waterline dry first if eyes water.[1]

Ophthalmology studies of eyeliner more broadly report associations with tear film and gland measures. A 2018 review concluded eyeliner applied at the inner lash line is associated with more tear-film contamination and discomfort than application on outer periocular skin.[4] A 2022 cross-sectional study of 220 women found shorter tear break-up time and more meibomian gland loss in eyeliner and mascara wearers than in women wearing no makeup.[4] A 2025 public survey found dry-eye symptom scores at or above a threshold in 42.9 percent of eyeliner users versus 33.4 percent of non-users, and 48.2 percent for lid-margin application; and a 2026 observational study of 49 people found worse meibomian gland excreta grades in frequent lid-margin eyeliner wearers than in rare makeup users, with no difference in tear break-up time.[4] These studies did not separate pale from dark liner.

No studies found on the cosmetic effect of light waterline liner. A pediatric dermatology report described using a white eyeliner pencil to mark capillary malformations before laser treatment, a medical use unrelated to cosmetic eye brightening.[5]

lore.intro: Claims about pale waterline liner come mainly from makeup artists, brand beauty magazines and tutorials rather than from forum threads.[1][2]
